# The Great North Road: A Journey Through Memory and Landscape

The poem opens by addressing the Great North Road as though it were an old and trusted friend, greeting it with the familiarity born of long acquaintance. As the verse traces the road's steady westward journey, it evokes the countless memorable sunsets that have accompanied this passage—each one a small ceremony marking the day's end and the traveller's progress. In this way, the road becomes more than mere infrastructure; it is a companion whose company the speaker has kept across many years and many crossings.

Woven into this greeting are the speaker's earliest recollections. Childhood visits to Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy, who lived in their council flat on Karangahape Road, first opened the speaker's eyes to the grandeur of New Zealand's far north. These family journeys, undertaken with the wide-eyed wonder of youth, planted the seeds of a lifelong attachment to the landscape. What began as simple visits to relatives became formative encounters with a vast and beautiful country, and the memory of that early astonishment lingers throughout the poem.

Central to the work is the vivid personification of the road itself, which the speaker imagines as a "sleek black eel." This striking image transforms the highway into something living and sinuous, a dark and glistening creature that carries life and movement between Karangahape Road and the wild western beaches. Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells, and Piha are named like a litany of beloved destinations, each one a jewel at the road's western reach. The eel-like road threads them together, pulsing with the traffic of human comings and goings, forever channelling energy from the city outward to the sea.

As the poem develops, the speaker turns to a quieter, more reflective register, contemplating the passage of time. Where once the years seemed to stretch endlessly ahead, they now appear to overtake the speaker with every journey back and forth along the familiar route. The road that once witnessed a child's wonder has become the measure of a life advancing, and each trip carries with it an awareness of how swiftly the seasons accumulate. There is both tenderness and melancholy in this recognition—the sense that the road endures while the traveller ages.

Finally, the poem closes on a note of celebration and gentle urging, issuing calls to protect the natural world. The speaker implores the road to keep saving the whales and to go on preserving the hidden toheroa buried beneath the western sands. In these closing lines, the personified road is entrusted with a guardian's role, becoming a symbol of continuity and care. The poem thus ends not in nostalgia alone, but in hope—a plea that the beauty of the far north, its creatures and its coastlines, might be safeguarded for the journeys still to come.

# Great North Road

There's a particular kind of intimacy we develop with the roads of our childhood—the ones that carried us, again and again, toward the people and places that shaped us. This poem takes such a road, Auckland's Great North Road, and speaks to it not as an inert stretch of asphalt but as a living companion, a friend who has witnessed the unfolding of a life. In doing so, it transforms an ordinary thoroughfare into something tender and mythic, a thread stitching together memory, geography, and time.

The poem opens in the register of direct address, speaking to the road as one might speak to an old confidant. Here the speaker returns in memory to the visits of childhood—the journeys made to see relatives scattered across the region, the anticipation of arrival, the familiar landmarks that marked the way. These recollections are not merely nostalgic; they establish the road as a keeper of history, a witness to family gatherings and the small rituals of belonging. Every bend and rise carries the residue of a child's excitement, the backseat impatience, the slow accumulation of a sense of home.

As the poem moves outward, its imagery turns toward the coast. The beaches of New Zealand's north rise into view—their black sands, their restless tides, the meeting place of land and ocean. This coastal imagery does more than decorate the poem; it gestures toward the deeper rhythms of the natural world, the vastness against which human lives are measured. The journey along the road becomes a passage not only through space but through time, tracing the distance between who we were and who we have become.

At the heart of the poem lies its central and most striking image: the road as a "sleek black eel." The metaphor is remarkably apt. Like an eel, the road is dark, sinuous, and alive—winding its way through the landscape with a fluid, almost animal grace. The eel is also a creature of both fresh and salt water, a natural traveller between inland streams and the open sea, and so the image binds together the poem's dual poles of city and coast. The road, like the eel, is life-giving, a channel through which movement, connection, and vitality flow. It links the urban world of Auckland to the wild edges of the ocean, refusing to let them remain separate.

Through this affectionate tribute, the poem arrives at its larger meditation. It celebrates the enduring bonds that hold a life together—the bond between people who travel to reach one another, between the individual and the particular place that raised them, and between human beings and the natural landscape that surrounds and sustains them. The passage of time, so often a source of grief, is here softened by continuity: the road remains, the beaches remain, and the memories they hold remain accessible to anyone willing to travel back along them.

In the end, the poem offers something quietly profound. By personifying the Great North Road, it reminds us that the places we move through are never neutral. They gather our histories, carry our journeys, and connect us—city to sea, past to present, one person to another. The road is a friend precisely because it endures, faithfully linking the disparate parts of a life and of a landscape into a single, continuous whole.

# The Dog's Bollocks

"The dog's bollocks" is one of the more colourful expressions in British slang, used to describe something that is excellent, first-rate, or the very best of its kind. Despite its crude-sounding components, the phrase is generally considered a term of high praise. Calling something "the dog's bollocks" means it's outstanding—the finest example you could hope to find.

## Meaning and Usage

The expression functions as an enthusiastic compliment. You might hear someone say, "That new restaurant is the dog's bollocks," meaning it's absolutely brilliant. It sits alongside similar British phrases like "the bee's knees" or "the cat's whiskers," all of which express admiration by referencing an animal's body part in a whimsical way.

The phrase is informal and can sound vulgar in polite company, so it tends to appear in casual conversation among friends rather than in formal settings.

## Origins

The exact origins of the phrase are debated, but several theories exist. One popular explanation suggests it emerged from typography and printing, where the punctuation mark ":-" was jokingly called a "dog's bollocks." Another theory ties it to the broader tradition of animal-based slang that flourished in the early twentieth century.

The expression gained wider recognition in the latter half of the 1900s and remains a staple of British and Australian vernacular today.

## Cultural Notes

For those unfamiliar with British slang, the positive meaning can be surprising. In many contexts, references to bodily parts carry negative connotations, but here the phrase paradoxically signals excellence. This quirk makes it a favourite example of how English idioms can defy literal interpretation.

Understanding expressions like "the dog's bollocks" offers a small window into the playful, irreverent character of British English.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem addressed to Great North Road in Auckland as if it were an old friend, mixing nostalgia, New Zealand slang, and references to the west coast beaches like Piha and Karekare.
counterfactuals.output:
To Great North Road

Kia ora, old mate, you long grey ribbon,
still winding out through Grey Lynn's villas,
past the dairies and the op-shops
where I spent my student years half-broke,
counting coins for a mince pie and a L&P.

Remember, eh? How we'd load the Corolla,
boards on the roof, jandals in the footwell,
and you'd carry us westward like an old dog
who knows the way without being told,
out past Waterview, out toward the ranges.

You were always the beginning of something.
The tar seal warming under a nor'wester,
the smell of the bush getting greener,
until you handed us over to the winding roads
that spilled us down to Piha —
that black-sand cathedral, Lion Rock keeping watch,
the surf coming in hard as a hangi steaming,
sweet as.

Or Karekare, quieter, where the water
laid itself flat across the sand like glass,
and we'd walk out barefoot, sunburnt, salted,
talking rubbish and meaning every word of it.

You've changed, ay. New lights, new cafés,
the traffic thicker than it ever was,
but I still know your bones, old friend —
the way you dip and rise past Kingsland,
the graffiti walls, the rugby crowds,
the whole chaotic beautiful chur of you.

So here's to you, Great North Road.
You never asked for thanks,
just carried us out and brought us home,
every summer, every heartbreak,
every long slow drive back
with sand still in our hair
and the west coast sun
going down behind us
like a mate waving goodbye.

Ka kite, old road.
Ka kite anō.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse ode to a famous New Zealand road, personifying it and weaving in memories of childhood visits to relatives on K'Road, plus references to whales, toheroas, and surfing culture.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ode to State Highway One

You old grey ribbon, you unspooling thing,
I have known you longer than my own name.
You carried me north in the back of a Holden,
carsick and dreaming, my forehead
against the glass, watching the Waikato blur
into something like memory before it happened.

*

Auckland rising, and there you'd tighten,
narrow into that other artery—
Karangahape, K'Road—
where my aunty lived above a shop
that smelled of frying and incense and someone
else's grandmother's cooking.
You brought me to her doorstep every summer,
you patient road, you keeper of arrivals.

The neon there was a language I couldn't read,
the streetwalkers kind to a child too small
to understand their kindness,
and my cousins and I ran the footpath cracks
like they were rivers we could fall into.

*

But you are more than the city's held breath.

You stretch me back toward the sea,
where the toheroa once lay thick as coins
in the wet sand at Ninety Mile,
and the old ones bent to gather them—
that green soup, that taste of buried tide—
before the beds thinned out to almost-nothing,
before *plenty* became a story
we tell to prove it happened.

*

I have followed you to where the water darkens
and the whales pass like slow grey thoughts,
migratory, ancient, minding their own business
beneath the churn—
southern rights and humpbacks
tracing their own long highways,
older than yours, unpaved, unnumbered,
the sea's memory of where to go.

*

And you know the surf towns too,
the Raglan boys with salt-stiff hair
waxing their boards at dawn,
the left-hand break unrolling like your own
long tar horizon—
that same forever-motion,
that same promise of *around the next bend,
just wait, just keep going.*

*

So here is my ode, you humble spine of the country:
you who held my childhood in your lanes,
who smelled of hot bitumen and the sea both at once,
who took me to my people and brought me home again—

I am still driving you.
I am always, in some part of me,
carsick and eight years old,
watching the whole green world go by
and trusting you to know the way.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece that celebrates Great North Road in Auckland, blending Kiwi cultural references, environmental themes, and personal family history into a heartfelt address.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Road That Made Us

*A heartfelt address*

---

Friends, family, neighbours—kia ora koutou.

I want to talk to you today about a road. Not just any road, but *our* road. Great North Road. The long grey ribbon that unspools through the heart of Auckland, from the city out west toward the ranges, carrying with it a hundred and fifty years of stories—and every single one of my family's among them.

My grandmother used to say that Great North Road had two faces. In the morning, when the light came up over the harbour, it was a road of promise—of people heading to work, of buses groaning up the rise past Grey Lynn, of pōhutukawa flaring red against the sky like the land itself was applauding the summer. And in the evening, it was a road of homecoming. Of the same tired faces heading back. Of fish and chips wrapped in paper, eaten on the tailgate of a ute. Of coming home.

She would know. She raised six children in a villa off that road, back when Grey Lynn was cheap and Pasifika and Māori families made it sing. She'd tell me about the churches on Sunday, the sound of hymns in three languages drifting out the open windows. About the corner dairy where the whole neighbourhood was known by name and a kid could get a bag of mixed lollies for twenty cents and a smile.

---

But I don't want to romanticise it. Great North Road has known hard times too. It has seen the arterial roar of traffic choke the air where tūī once sang. It has watched the creeks that fed into the Waitematā run grey with runoff. It has seen the great old trees felled for another lane, another development, another promise that wasn't always kept.

And this is where I ask something of us.

Because a road is not just tarmac. It is a living corridor. Along Great North Road there are efforts now—community plantings, the slow return of native green, the restoration of the streams that our tūpuna knew by name. When we plant a kōwhai on that verge, we are not just landscaping. We are apologising to the whenua. We are saying: *we remember what was here, and we will make room for it again.*

My grandfather planted a lemon tree in that villa garden in 1961. It's still there. Different family owns the house now, but that tree has fed strangers for sixty years. That's what we leave on a road like this. Not our names—those wash away. But the living things we set into the ground.

---

So here is my hope.

That the children walking Great North Road today—past the murals, past the op shops and the new cafés, past the mosque and the marae and the corner where my grandmother's dairy used to be—that they inherit not just the concrete, but the care.

That they hear the tūī returning.

That they know a road is only as good as the community that walks it, and that the truest measure of a place is whether it makes room for everyone: the old families and the new, the land and the people, the past and whatever comes next.

Great North Road made us. Let us, in turn, be worthy of it.

Kia ora, and thank you.

---

counterfactuals.label: cf_4

*Dear you, wherever the plane spat you out—*

Listen: the motorway has grown a spine again.
Northwestern, that sleek black eel,
slid up out of Te Atatū this morning
tasting the harbour on her lip,
all her scales the wet-shine of after-rain,
and she wanted me to tell you—

*(she cannot write, she has no hands,
only lanes, only the long muscle of going)*

—that she misses you.

                              She said it in traffic.
She said it in the merge past Lincoln Road
where she coils, where she thickens,
belly full of Henderson,
belly full of everyone leaving for the day.

Friend, you would not believe how she's changed.
She used to be a shy creek-thing,
a tuna in the raupō down by Oratia,
and now—look—she muscles clean through New Lynn,
she elbows Great North Road,
she drinks the tunnel light and hums.

At night she is at her most herself:
a long black gloss, a gleaming want,
tail-flick toward Waitākere,
head resting cool in the city's cupped palm.
I drive her ribs at eleven
and she lets me. She purrs. Affection
is just friction we agree to call warm.

*Things I am supposed to relay, per the eel:*
— that Scenic Drive still curls its finger at the ranges
— that Piha keeps the black sand you licked from your teeth
— that the Glen Eden underpass smells of you, somehow, of that year
— that she has kept a lane open. She wants you to know
                                                                             she has kept a lane.

So here is the strange soft thing:
I think a road can love the way an eel loves—
which is to say by *route*, by return,
by nosing back always to the same dark water.
You are her Manukau. You are her mouth of the harbour.
Wherever you spill out at last, she is pointed there.

Come home along her.
She'll carry you gentle from Waitākere to the sea,
sleek and black and glad,
and I will be standing at Te Atatū
where the eel begins,
waving like an idiot,
saying *look, look, she remembered you,*

                                                            *she remembered.*

*— me, & the motorway, & all of West Auckland holding its breath*
